chapter_note.about: A context-free grammar rewrites one variable at a time, and a pushdown automaton adds a stack to a finite automaton. They describe the same languages. This chapter starts with derivations, parse trees and ambiguity, then shows how to name the language of a grammar and design a grammar for a given language. After that come PDA moves and acceptance, the deterministic versus non-deterministic split, closure properties, Chomsky and Greibach normal forms, CYK parsing, and count invariants. Most questions ask you to name a language, decide whether it is context-free or deterministic, or use a closure fact.
chapter_note.simple: A grammar is a recipe book for building words by swapping capital letters for other letters, and a pushdown automaton is a machine with a pile of plates that checks words by pushing and popping. Both can handle things that nest, like matching brackets, which a plain finite automaton cannot. You learn to build words by following rules, to see when a word can be built in two different ways (ambiguity), and to say what family of words a recipe makes. You also learn which tricks keep you inside the family (gluing, repeating, reading backwards) and which do not (asking for words that pass two checks at once). In exam words: CFG, parse tree, ambiguity, PDA, DPDA versus NPDA, closure, CNF, GNF, CYK and count invariants.

cards.title: Grammars and derivations
cards.simple: A grammar is a list of rewriting rules, like a recipe book for building sentences. You start with one special word, S, and each rule lets you swap one capitalised word for a mix of ordinary letters and other capitalised words. You keep swapping until only ordinary letters are left. The finished string is a member of the language. You can swap the leftmost capitalised word each time (a leftmost derivation) or the rightmost; the result is the same family of strings. In exam words: a context-free grammar derives strings by replacing one variable at a time, and its language is the set of all terminal strings derivable from the start symbol.
cards.idea: A **context-free grammar** is a set of rewriting rules. Start with the start symbol S and, at each step, replace **one variable** by the right side of one of its rules. When only terminals remain, you have derived a string. The language of the grammar is the set of all strings you can derive this way.
cards.definition:
A CFG is (V, Σ, P, S): variables V, terminals Σ, rules P of the form A → α with A a variable and α a string of variables and terminals, and a start symbol S.

- One derivation step: αAβ ⇒ αγβ when A → γ is a rule.
- A leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable, a rightmost derivation the rightmost.
- L(G) = { w in Σ* : S ⇒* w }.
cards.intuition_full: A derivation is a recipe execution: each step uses one rule on one variable and leaves everything else alone. When a form contains several variables, you may pick any of them, and the order does not change what can be produced, only the bookkeeping. Fixing the order (always leftmost, or always rightmost) gives each parse tree exactly one derivation of each kind, which is why 'ambiguous' can be defined with either. The length of a derivation is the number of rule uses. In this grammar, to produce a^m b^n you use S → AB once, A → aA (m−1) times and A → a once, B → bB (n−1) times and B → b once.

examples.setup: G has the rules S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. Derive aabb by a leftmost derivation. How many steps does it take?
steps: Grammar G: S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. A derivation starts at the start symbol S and replaces one variable per step. Goal: derive aabb.
Step 1: S → AB. The form now has two variables, A and B.
Step 2: a leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable. That is A, and we use A → aA.
Step 3: the leftmost variable is still A. Use A → a to finish it.
Step 4: now the only variable is B. Use B → bB.
Step 5: B → b. No variables are left, so aabb is derived in 5 steps and aabb is in L(G). This grammar generates a⁺b⁺: one or more a's, then one or more b's.
examples.answer: S ⇒ AB ⇒ aAB ⇒ aaB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb: 5 steps.

examples.setup: G: S → aSb | SS | ε. Is abab in L(G)? Is ba? What kind of strings does G generate?
steps: Every use of S → aSb puts an a on the left and a b on the right, around whatever S derives. So a is always matched with a later b, like '(' and ')'.
abab: S ⇒ SS ⇒ aSbS ⇒ abS ⇒ abaSb ⇒ abab, using S → SS, S → aSb, S → ε, S → aSb, S → ε. That is 5 steps.
ba is not derivable: no rule can put a b before the a it is matched with.
So L(G) is the set of balanced bracket strings with a as '(' and b as ')'. Checking every string up to length 10 confirms it.
examples.answer: abab is in L(G), ba is not. L(G) = balanced a/b strings (every prefix has at least as many a's as b's, and the totals are equal).

examples.setup: For the basic grammar, write the rightmost derivation of aabb. Does it use different rules from the leftmost one?
steps: Rightmost means: always replace the rightmost variable.
S ⇒ AB. The rightmost variable is B: AB ⇒ AbB (B → bB), then AbB ⇒ Abb (B → b).
Now only A is left: Abb ⇒ aAbb (A → aA), then aAbb ⇒ aabb (A → a).
The same five rules were used, only in a different order, and both derivations have the same parse tree.
examples.answer: S ⇒ AB ⇒ AbB ⇒ Abb ⇒ aAbb ⇒ aabb. Same rules, different order, same tree.

cards.why: Everything else in this chapter (parse trees, ambiguity, naming a language, normal forms) is built on derivations. In GATE: decide whether a string is derivable, name the language of a small grammar, or count derivation steps.
how: Start from S and write the current form after each step.
At each step name the variable you replace and the rule you use.
Stop when no variable remains. That string is in the language.
To show a string is not derivable, find an invariant that every derivable string keeps and this one breaks.
cards.mistake: Replacing more than one variable in a single step, or treating a derivation as a fixed list of strings. One step rewrites exactly one variable. Another slip is to confuse the grammar with the language: two different grammars can generate the same language.
edge_cases: The empty string is derivable only if S ⇒* ε, for example through S → ε.
A variable with no terminating rule produces no strings, so its rules are useless.
A derivation of a string of length n can have many more than n steps, because variables and ε-rules also take steps.
connections: The same derivation drawn as a tree is a parse tree (next card).
Reading what each rule adds gives the language of a grammar (card 3).

cards.title: Parse trees and ambiguity
cards.simple: When you read the sentence 'I saw the man with the telescope', you can picture two different stories: either I used a telescope, or the man had one. The words are identical but the grouping changes the meaning. A parse tree is a picture of one such grouping. If you can draw two different grouping pictures for the same string, the grammar is ambiguous. In arithmetic, 2+3*4 can mean 20 or 14 depending on the grouping, which is exactly why compilers use a grammar with precedence built in. In exam words: a grammar is ambiguous if some string has two different parse trees (or two leftmost derivations).
cards.idea: A **parse tree** shows how a derivation groups a string: the root is S, each inner node is a variable with the rule's right side as children, and the leaves read the string. A grammar is **ambiguous** if some string has two different parse trees. Ambiguity belongs to the grammar, not the language.
cards.definition:
A parse tree for G has root S, internal nodes labelled by variables whose children spell the right side of a rule, and leaves labelled by terminals (or ε). The yield is the leaves read left to right.

G is ambiguous if some w in L(G) has two different parse trees, equivalently two different leftmost derivations (or two rightmost). A language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar for it is ambiguous.
cards.intuition_full: Each parse tree corresponds to one leftmost derivation and vice versa, so counting trees counts leftmost derivations. Ambiguity is dangerous when the grouping carries meaning, as in expressions and in dangling-else. The grammar E → E+E | E*E | num has no notion of which operator binds tighter, so it allows both groupings. Layering the grammar (E for sums, T for products, F for atoms) forces * deeper in the tree than +, which removes the second tree. A short grammar can still be ambiguous, and a simple language can have an ambiguous grammar next to an unambiguous one. Only a string with two trees proves ambiguity.

examples.setup: G: E → E+E | E*E | num. Show that the input 2+3*4 has two parse trees, give their values, and fix the grammar.
steps: Grammar: E → E+E | E*E | num. Take the input 2+3*4. A parse tree shows which rules were applied and how the string is grouped.
Parse tree 1: the root uses E → E*E. Its left E derives 2+3 and its right E derives 4.
Read the leaves left to right: 2+3*4. The tree says to add first, so its value is (2 + 3) * 4 = 20.
Parse tree 2 for the same string: the root uses E → E+E, and its right E derives 3*4.
Its value is 2 + (3 * 4) = 14. One string has two parse trees and two meanings, so the grammar is ambiguous.
Fix it by building precedence into the grammar: E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → num. Now * can only sit lower in the tree than +, so only the 14-tree exists.
examples.answer: Two trees, with values 20 and 14, so G is ambiguous. The layered grammar E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → num has one tree.

examples.setup: G: S → aS | Sa | a. Is G ambiguous? Give a witness.
steps: Try the shortest strings. a has one tree: S → a.
aa, tree 1: S → aS, then the inner S → a. The second a comes from the inner S.
aa, tree 2: S → Sa, then the inner S → a. The first a comes from the inner S.
These are two different trees for aa, so G is ambiguous. A tree counter confirms exactly 2 trees for aa.
examples.answer: Ambiguous, with witness aa.

examples.setup: The language of G above is a⁺. Is a⁺ inherently ambiguous?
steps: Try the grammar S → aS | a for the same language.
Every string a^n has exactly one parse tree in it: a chain of S → aS ending with S → a.
So a⁺ has an unambiguous grammar, and ambiguity is a property of the grammar, not of the language.
examples.answer: No. Different grammars for the same language can differ in ambiguity.

cards.why: Ambiguity decides whether a grammar can be used for parsing, and it shows up as 'which grammar is ambiguous' questions. In GATE: find a string with two parse trees, count parse trees, or recognise the precedence-fixed grammar.
how: Look for a rule where the same variable can appear on both sides of the choice (E → E+E | E*E, S → SS).
Try the shortest string that uses two rules in two different orders.
Draw both trees or write both leftmost derivations. If they differ, the grammar is ambiguous.
To remove ambiguity, layer the grammar or force one associativity.
cards.mistake: Calling a grammar unambiguous because it is short or because its language looks simple. Ambiguity needs only one string with two trees, and the grammar can be ambiguous even if the language has an unambiguous grammar. Also, two derivations that differ only in order, not tree, do not count.
edge_cases: Two different derivations with the same tree are not ambiguity. Leftmost derivations are in 1-to-1 correspondence with trees.
S → SS | a gives many trees for a^n, one for each way to bracket the string.
Inherently ambiguous languages exist, for example {a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k}.
connections: Compilers use unambiguous grammars (parsing chapter); ambiguity shows up as shift-reduce conflicts in LR parsing.
Counting trees is the same idea as counting leftmost derivations (card 1).

check.q: Does ambiguity belong to the language or to the grammar?

cards.title: Language of a grammar
cards.simple: To work out what words a grammar makes, do not stare at the rules; run them. Pick a rule that has the start word in the middle, like aSc, and ask 'what does one use of this add to the string, and where?'. If a rule adds one letter on the left and one on the right, it builds matched pairs from the outside in. If a rule adds to only one end, it builds a plain run of letters. Once you know what each rule adds, you can write the pattern of the whole language. In exam words: find the language of a grammar by reading what each production contributes, then confirm with short derived strings.
cards.idea: To find the **language of a grammar**, ask what each rule adds and where. A rule like S → aSc adds an a on the left and a c on the right, so it builds matched pairs from the outside in. Track the counts of each letter, name the pattern, then confirm by deriving two or three short strings.
cards.definition:
For each rule A → α, note how many of each terminal it adds and whether they go left, right, or in the middle.

- A rule that wraps the variable (A → xAy) builds nested pairs.
- A rule that adds on one side (A → Ax) builds a run.
- A union of rules gives a union of cases.

The language is the set of all terminal strings derivable. Confirm the guess by checking short strings in both directions: derivable and non-derivable.
cards.intuition_full: Every derived string is built layer by layer, and the layers are decided by the rules in the order of use. Wrapping rules fix a relation between left and right ends, so the string has matched pairs. Rules that add on one side make a free run. The language is the product of these layers. When two kinds of pairs are nested (outer a-c, inner b-c), the counts add up: the number of c's is n + m. This is context-free because the pairs are nested, not crossing. Always test the guess against a string the guess excludes, because a language that is 'almost' your guess is the usual trap.

examples.setup: G: S → aSc | T and T → bTc | ε. What language does G generate? Derive abbccc as evidence.
steps: To name the language of a grammar, say what each rule adds. G: S → aSc | T and T → bTc | ε. We derive abbccc and watch the counts.
S → aSc adds an a on the left and a c on the right, around the rest. This is an outer pair, so n = 1.
S → T stops adding outer pairs. From now on only T is rewritten, in the middle.
T → bTc adds a b on the left and a c on the right of the rest: an inner pair, so m = 1. The c's are now 2.
Use T → bTc again: m = 2. The string is now abbTccc, with 1 a, 2 b's and 3 c's.
T → ε removes the last variable: abbccc. Every a and every b has its own c, so the c's number n + m. L = { a^n b^m c^(n+m) : n, m ≥ 0 }.
examples.answer: L = { a^n b^m c^(n+m) : n, m ≥ 0 }. For example S ⇒ aSc ⇒ aTc ⇒ abTcc ⇒ abbTccc ⇒ abbccc.

examples.setup: G: S → aSb | bSa | SS | ε. What is L(G)?
steps: Each rule adds exactly one a and one b (S → SS adds what its two halves add, ε adds nothing). So every derived string has #a = #b.
Is every string with #a = #b derivable? ba: S ⇒ bSa ⇒ ba. abba: S ⇒ SS ⇒ aSbS ⇒ abS ⇒ abbSa ⇒ abba.
A brute-force check of all strings up to length 10 shows the language is exactly the strings with equal numbers of a's and b's.
So L(G) = { w : #a(w) = #b(w) }, not just a^n b^n.

examples.setup: Remove S → SS: G': S → aSb | bSa | ε. Is abba still derivable?
steps: Without SS, every derivation wraps: the outermost pair is an a with a b, or a b with an a.
So the first and last symbols of every derived string differ, and the same holds for the pair inside, and so on: w_i ≠ w_(n+1−i) for every i.
abba starts and ends with a, so it cannot be derived. abab can: a, then bSa → ba, then b gives abab.
examples.answer: No. L(G') = even-length strings whose i-th symbol differs from the i-th symbol from the end.

cards.mistake: Judging a language from one or two derived strings. The string ab is in a^n b^n and in many other languages. Test a string the guess excludes, and check what happens when every rule is used more than once.

S → SS makes a concatenation of languages: strings of balanced blocks.
Two variables can nest to give a^n b^m c^(n+m), still context-free.

For each rule A → α, note how many of each terminal it adds and whether they go left, right, or in the middle.

- A rule that wraps the variable (A → xAy) builds nested pairs.
- A rule that adds on one side (A → Ax) builds a run.
- A union of rules gives a union of cases.

The language is the set of all terminal strings derivable. Confirm the guess by checking short strings in both directions: derivable and non-derivable.

1. To name the language of a grammar, say what each rule adds. G: S → aSc | T and T → bTc | ε. We derive abbccc and watch the counts.
2. S → aSc adds an a on the left and a c on the right, around the rest. This is an outer pair, so n = 1.
3. S → T stops adding outer pairs. From now on only T is rewritten, in the middle.
4. T → bTc adds a b on the left and a c on the right of the rest: an inner pair, so m = 1. The c's are now 2.

6. T → ε removes the last variable: abbccc. Every a and every b has its own c, so the c's number n + m. L = { a^n b^m c^(n+m) : n, m ≥ 0 }.

cards.simple: Writing a grammar is like writing building instructions for a particular kind of word. If the word needs two parts to match in size, you write a rule that adds one of each at the same time, on the two sides, and keep repeating it. cards.title: PDA moves and acceptance
cards.simple: A pushdown automaton is a small machine with a pile of plates next to it. It reads the word one letter at a time, and on each step it looks at the top plate, may take it off, and may put new plates on. With the pile it can remember things in order, for example 'I have seen a then b', and later undo them in reverse order, which is perfect for matching brackets. The word is accepted when the machine ends in a special finish state, or, in the other version, when the pile is completely empty. In exam words: a PDA move reads an input symbol (or ε), pops the top, and pushes a string; acceptance is by final state or by empty stack.
cards.idea: A **PDA** is a finite automaton with a **stack**. Each move reads one input symbol (or none), looks at the top of the stack, pops it, and pushes a string of symbols. It accepts either when it ends in a **final state** or when the stack is **empty**. The two modes recognise the same languages.
cards.definition:
A move δ(q, a, X) = {(p, γ)} means: in state q, reading input a (or ε) with X on top, go to p, replace X by the string γ (leftmost symbol on top).

A configuration is (state, unread input, stack). A string is accepted if some computation reads all the input and then either is in a final state (final-state acceptance) or has an empty stack (empty-stack acceptance).

Pushing nothing (γ = ε) is a pop. Pushing X together with something else keeps X.
cards.intuition_full: The stack is the memory that makes nested matching possible: push when you open, pop when you close. For w c w^R, the first half is pushed, so the stack holds it reversed, and the second half pops it in exactly the order it needs to match. The marker c tells the machine when to switch. Tracing a PDA is bookkeeping with three columns: state, remaining input, stack. A final-state PDA may leave symbols on the stack when it accepts, while an empty-stack PDA must clear everything, including the bottom marker. Both models accept exactly the context-free languages, and converting between them only needs a few extra moves.

examples.setup: A PDA has states q0 (start), q1, q2 (final). In q0, reading a or b, it pushes A or B on top of the stack. In q0, reading c, it goes to q1 without changing the stack. In q1, reading a with A on top, or b with B on top, it pops. In q1, with ⊥ on top, an ε-move goes to q2. Trace the input abcba.
steps: This PDA accepts { w c w^R }. State q0 pushes the first half, the symbol c switches to q1, and q1 matches the second half by popping. q2 is final. Input abcba, stack ⊥. A configuration is (state, unread input, stack with the top first).
Read a in q0: push A. The stack, top first, is A⊥.
Read b in q0: push B. The stack is BA⊥.
Read c: go to q1. The stack does not change, since c marks the middle.
Read b in q1 with B on top: they match, so pop B. The stack is A⊥.
Read a with A on top: they match, so pop A. The stack is ⊥ and the input is empty.
With the input used up and ⊥ on top, the ε-move goes to q2, a final state. Accepted, by final state.
examples.answer: Accepted. The configurations run (q0, abcba, ⊥) → (q0, bcba, A⊥) → (q0, cba, BA⊥) → (q1, ba, BA⊥) → (q1, a, A⊥) → (q1, ε, ⊥) → (q2, ε, ⊥).

examples.setup: A PDA accepts by final state, with finals q0 and q1. Moves: in q0, reading a with ⊥ or A on top, push A. In q0, reading b with A on top, pop and go to q1. In q1, reading b with A on top, pop. No other moves. What language does it accept?
steps: Each a pushes one A. Each b pops one A, and the first b moves to q1.
Acceptance is by final state, and both q0 and q1 are final. The stack does not have to be empty.
aaabb: push 3 A's, pop 2, end in q1. Accepted, with one A left over.
aabbb: the third b finds ⊥ on top and there is no move, so the run dies. Rejected. Also, a's cannot follow b's, because q1 has no move on a.
examples.answer: L = { a^n b^m : 0 ≤ m ≤ n }. Brute force over all strings up to length 9 confirms it.

examples.setup: Keep those moves but accept by empty stack (no finals) and add ε-moves that pop ⊥ in q0 and in q1. What language does it accept now?
steps: Now the only way to empty the stack is to pop ⊥, which needs ⊥ on top.
⊥ is on top only when every A has been popped, that is, when the number of b's equals the number of a's.
So the same moves now accept exactly the strings a^n b^n.
examples.answer: L = { a^n b^n : n ≥ 0 }. The acceptance mode changes the language, so read it before reading the moves.

cards.title: DPDA versus NPDA
cards.simple: Imagine reading a word letter by letter and putting plates on a pile. At some moment you have to stop piling and start matching plates against the letters. If the word contains a clear signal, like a whistle at the exact middle, you know when to switch. If there is no whistle, you cannot tell: the same few starting letters might be the first half of a short word or just the beginning of a long one, and you cannot see the future. A machine that always has one right move is called deterministic. A machine that may guess and try both options is non-deterministic. In exam words: DPDA languages are a strict subset of CFLs, and languages like ww^R need non-determinism because the middle has no marker.
cards.idea: A **deterministic PDA** has at most one move in every situation. The languages it accepts, the **DCFLs**, are a strict subset of the context-free languages. A language needs non-determinism when the machine must **guess a boundary**, such as the middle of ww^R. With a marker, such as the c in wcw^R, the guess disappears.
cards.definition:
A PDA is deterministic if for every state q, input symbol a and stack top X, at most one move applies, counting ε-moves (an ε-move on (q, X) rules out any other move on (q, X)).

Facts: DCFL ⊂ CFL strictly. Examples: a^n b^n, w c w^R, a^n b^n c^m are DCFLs; w w^R and a^n b^n ∪ a^n b^2n are CFLs but not DCFLs; a^n b^n c^n is not even a CFL. DCFLs are closed under complement but not under union or intersection.
cards.intuition_full: The reason is information. A PDA reads left to right and has only the stack to remember things. At the middle of ww^R it must switch from pushing to popping, but the middle is not marked and depends on the whole length, which it has not seen. Two inputs can share a long prefix yet need the switch at different places, and a deterministic machine has to choose before it can tell them apart. An NPDA avoids the problem by trying both. A marker or a fixed shape (a^n b^n) tells the DPDA exactly when to switch, so such languages are deterministic. Complement works for DCFLs because a DPDA can be completed and its acceptance flipped; union fails because combining two deterministic machines forces a guess about which one to follow.

examples.setup: Take L = {w w^R : w in {a, b}*}. Show with the two members abba and abbbba why a deterministic PDA cannot accept L.
steps: L = {w w^R} is the even palindromes, with no marker in the middle. Take two members: abba and abbbba. Is there a deterministic way to read them?
A deterministic PDA pushes as it reads. After the first two symbols, a and b, the stack holds ⊥ a b with b on top, for both inputs.
The third symbol is b, equal to the top. In abba this b opens the second half, so the machine must pop.
In abbbba the very same b is still in the first half, since the middle comes after 3 symbols. Here the machine must push.
Up to this symbol the two inputs look identical (a, b, b), yet they need opposite moves. A deterministic machine must commit without seeing the future, so it fails on one of them.

An NPDA guesses the middle: it tries both moves and accepts if one branch works. So {w w^R} is context-free but not a DCFL. With a marker, {w c w^R}, the choice disappears and the PDA is deterministic.
examples.answer: After reading abb, the machine must pop for abba and push for abbbba. The prefix is the same and the required moves differ, so L is not a DCFL (but an NPDA accepts it by guessing).

examples.setup: Classify each language as DCFL, CFL but not DCFL, or not CFL: (a) {a^n b^n}  (b) {w c w^R}  (c) {w w^R}  (d) {a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k}  (e) {a^n b^n c^n}
steps: (a) The stack counts the a's and cancels with the b's. The switch happens at the first b, so it is deterministic: DCFL.
(b) The marker c tells the machine exactly when to stop pushing and start popping: DCFL.
(c) No marker, so the middle must be guessed: CFL but not DCFL.
(d) After reading a's and b's the machine does not know whether to compare a with b or b with c, and it cannot keep both: CFL but not DCFL.
(e) Three counts tied to each other need more than one stack: not context-free.
examples.answer: (a) DCFL, (b) DCFL, (c) CFL not DCFL, (d) CFL not DCFL, (e) not CFL.

cards.title: CFL closure
cards.simple: Think of context-free languages as words a machine with one pile of plates can check. If you glue two such languages together, join them with 'or', repeat them, or read them backwards, a single pile still does the job, so the result is still in the club. The trouble starts when you ask for words that pass two pile-based checks at once. Each check uses the pile for a different comparison, and a word like 'aaabbbccc' needs three counts to agree, which one pile cannot do. These need not be: L1 ∩ L2, the complement of L1, and L1 − L2 (take L1 = Σ*: then L1 − L2 is the complement of L2).

Proof ideas: union and concatenation combine grammars (new start rule). Intersection with a regular language runs a PDA and a DFA together. Non-closure under intersection uses aⁿbⁿcⁿ, and non-closure under complement follows by De Morgan.

cards.title: CNF and GNF
cards.simple: A normal form is like a tidy way of writing instructions, where every rule has to follow a strict shape. In Chomsky form every rule either swaps one capital letter for exactly two capital letters, or swaps one capital letter for one small letter. That tidy shape makes counting easy: to build a word of length n, you use n 'small letter' rules and n minus 1 'split in two' rules, so exactly 2n minus 1 steps. In Greibach form every rule starts with a small letter, so each step creates one small letter of the word, and the word takes n steps. In exam words: CNF has rules A → BC or A → a, giving derivations of 2n − 1 steps; GNF has rules A → aα, giving n steps.
cards.idea: A grammar in **Chomsky normal form** (CNF) has only rules A → BC and A → a. A grammar in **Greibach normal form** (GNF) has only rules A → aα, where α is a string of variables. CNF turns every derivation of a string of length n into exactly **2n − 1 steps**. GNF makes it exactly **n steps**.
cards.definition:
CNF: every rule is A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal), plus S → ε if ε is in the language. To convert: remove ε-rules, remove unit rules (A → B), replace terminals in long rules by variables, and split long right-hand sides into pairs.

GNF: every rule is A → aα with a a terminal and α a (possibly empty) string of variables.

Step counts for w with |w| = n ≥ 1: CNF takes n − 1 binary steps plus n terminal steps = 2n − 1. GNF takes n steps, one terminal per step.
cards.intuition_full: A CNF parse tree is a full binary tree: each inner node has exactly two children, and each leaf is a terminal. A full binary tree with n leaves has n − 1 inner nodes, and each inner node and each leaf-producing rule is one step, giving 2n − 1 steps in total. GNF fixes the order differently: every rule creates a terminal at the front, so each step adds exactly one letter of the string, and the remaining variables wait to produce the rest. The conversion order matters: remove ε first, then unit rules, then fix terminals and length. The language stays the same, apart from ε, which is handled separately.

examples.setup: Convert G: S → aSb | ab to Chomsky normal form and count the steps to derive aabb. Then count the steps in a Greibach normal form grammar.
steps: Original grammar G: S → aSb | ab. Chomsky normal form (CNF) allows only rules A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal).
Step 1: give each terminal its own variable, A → a and B → b. The rules become S → ASB | AB, A → a, B → b.
Step 2: break the long rule ASB into pieces of two variables with X → SB, so S → AX. CNF: S → AX | AB, X → SB, A → a, B → b.
Derive aabb in the CNF grammar. Steps 1 to 3: S ⇒ AX ⇒ aX ⇒ aSB. The form is a S B after 3 steps.
Steps 4 and 5: aSB ⇒ aABB ⇒ aaBB, using S → AB and then A → a.
Steps 6 and 7: aaBB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb. Total 7 = 2n − 1 for n = 4: three binary steps (n − 1) and four terminal steps (n).
Greibach normal form (GNF) needs every rule to start with a terminal: S → aSB | aB, B → b. Each step now produces one terminal, so aabb takes 4 steps: S ⇒ aSB ⇒ aaBB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb.
examples.answer: CNF: S → AX | AB, X → SB, A → a, B → b, and aabb takes 7 steps (2n − 1). GNF: S → aSB | aB, B → b, and aabb takes 4 steps (n).

examples.setup: A grammar in Chomsky normal form derives a string w in 31 steps. How long is w, and how many steps would a Greibach normal form grammar for the same language need?

2n − 1 = 31 gives n = 16.
In GNF each step produces exactly one terminal, so the same string takes n = 16 steps.
The count depends only on the length of the string, not on the number of variables.
examples.answer: |w| = 16, and GNF needs 16 steps.

examples.setup: Convert S → AB, A → a | ε, B → b to a grammar with no ε-rule and no unit rule.

S → B is a unit rule. Replace B by its right-hand side b: S → b.
Result: S → AB | b, A → a, B → b. It generates {ab, b}, the same as the original.

cards.title: CYK
cards.simple: CYK is a way to check whether a word fits a grammar by building up from small pieces. First you work out what each single letter can be. Then for every two-letter piece you try all the ways to cut it into two single letters and check whether some rule combines them. Then three-letter pieces, which you can cut in two ways, and so on up to the whole word. You write the results in a triangle of boxes, and if the box for the whole word contains the start symbol, the word belongs to the language. In exam words: CYK fills a triangular table bottom-up for a grammar in CNF, with n(n+1)/2 cells and O(n³) work, and accepts when the start symbol is in the top cell.
cards.idea: **CYK** decides whether a string belongs to a CNF grammar's language. Fill a triangle bottom-up: the cell for each substring holds the variables that derive it, found by combining two smaller cells with a rule X → YZ. Accept if the start symbol is in the cell for the whole string. The work is O(n³).
cards.definition:
For w = w1 … wn and a CNF grammar, let T[i, l] be the set of variables deriving the substring of length l starting at position i.

- l = 1: T[i, 1] = { X : X → wi is a rule }.
- l ≥ 2: T[i, l] = { X : X → YZ is a rule with Y in T[i, k] and Z in T[i + k, l − k] for some split k = 1 … l − 1 }.
- w is in L(G) if and only if S is in T[1, n].

Cells: n(n+1)/2. Split checks: for each length l, (n − l + 1)(l − 1), a total of C(n + 1, 3).
cards.intuition_full: Every string of length l ≥ 2 derived from a CNF variable splits at the root into two shorter substrings, each derived from one variable. So to know which variables derive a long substring, you only need the answers for its shorter pieces, which is dynamic programming over lengths. The table is a triangle because the substrings of length l start at n − l + 1 places. For each cell you try every cut point, which gives the cubic bound. Empty cells (∅) are normal and stop that branch. CNF is needed so that every rule splits into exactly two parts.

examples.setup: CNF grammar: S → AB | SS | AC, C → SB, A → a, B → b. Use CYK to decide whether aabb is in the language.
steps: CNF grammar: S → AB | SS | AC, C → SB, A → a, B → b. Input aabb, n = 4. Row l of the table is for substrings of length l. A cell holds the variables that derive that substring.
Length 1: a cell holds the variables with a rule X → terminal. Each a gives {A} and each b gives {B}.
Length 2: split into 1 + 1 and look for a rule X → YZ. aa: A A has no rule, so ∅. ab: A B gives S, so {S}. bb: B B has no rule, so ∅.
Length 3: aab splits as a|ab = A,S and aa|b = ∅,B. No rule X → A S, so ∅. abb splits as a|bb = A,∅ and ab|b = S,B, and C → SB gives {C}.
Length 4: aabb splits as a|abb = A,C and S → AC gives S. The other splits, aa|bb and aab|b, contain ∅. So the cell is {S}.
The top cell contains S, so aabb is in the language. Cost for n = 4: n(n+1)/2 = 10 cells and 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 split checks. In general this is O(n³).
examples.answer: Yes. The top cell is {S}. The table has 10 cells and 10 split checks.

examples.setup: CYK is run on a string of length 8 with a CNF grammar. How many table cells are filled, and how many (substring, split point) pairs are checked in total?
steps: Cells: one for every substring, so 8 + 7 + … + 1 = 8 · 9 / 2 = 36.
A substring of length l has l − 1 split points, and there are 8 − l + 1 substrings of that length.
Check with the formula C(n + 1, 3) = C(9, 3) = 84, which is O(n³).
examples.answer: 36 cells and 84 split checks.

examples.setup: With the same grammar, is abba in the language? Fill the top cell.
steps: Length 1: A, B, B, A. Length 2: ab gives S, bb gives ∅, ba gives ∅ (no rule X → B A).
Length 3: abb gives C (S B), bba gives ∅.
Length 4: abba splits as a|bba = A,∅; ab|ba = S,∅; abb|a = C,A. No rule X → C A. The cell is ∅.
examples.answer: No. The top cell is ∅, so abba is not in the language.

how: Write the string and draw a triangle: n cells at the bottom, one at the top.

edge_cases: The empty string is handled separately, since the table has no cell for it.
A cell can hold several variables at once, if several rules apply.
If a variable occurs in the left part only through an ε-rule, CNF removes the problem before CYK starts.
connections: CYK needs CNF (previous card), which is why CNF conversion matters.

cards.title: Count invariants
cards.simple: Suppose you are filling a jar with red and blue marbles using a few allowed scoops. One scoop adds one red and two blue marbles, another adds one blue, and another adds nothing. Whatever order you use the scoops, you know something about the final jar: there are always at least twice as many blue as red, because every red comes with two blues. Working this out for each scoop gives rules that every possible jar obeys, and you can use them to rule out answer options without listing the language. In exam words: count what each production adds to the numbers of a's and b's, then derive relations such as n_b ≥ 2 n_a that hold for every generated string.
cards.idea: Instead of listing the language, work out what **each rule adds** to the counts n_a and n_b. Use each rule x, y, … times, and write n_a and n_b in terms of those numbers. Whatever relation or bound holds between them holds for **every** string in the language.
cards.definition:
For each rule A → α record (Δa, Δb), the number of a's and b's in α (variables contribute what they later produce). Suppose rule i is used k_i times in a derivation. Then

  n_a = Σ k_i Δa_i,   n_b = Σ k_i Δb_i,   with every k_i ≥ 0.

Eliminate the k_i to get relations such as n_b ≥ 2 n_a, (n_a + n_b) divisible by 3, or n_a ≤ 2 n_b. Such relations are necessary conditions: they rule strings out but do not prove membership.
cards.intuition_full: A derivation is just a list of rule uses, so the final counts are fixed by how many times each rule is used. A rule that adds the same amount of a's and b's keeps n_a = n_b. A rule that adds only b's creates a surplus of b's that is free. A rule that adds (1, 2) ties two b's to each a. The relation you get is a linear inequality or equality in the k_i. These relations tell you what the language cannot contain, which is exactly what 'which of the following holds for every string' questions need. They do not tell you the order of symbols, so counts alone never prove that a string is in the language.

examples.setup: G: S → aSbb | bS | ε. Which relation between n_a and n_b holds for every generated string? Derive abbb as an illustration.
steps: Grammar S → aSbb | bS | ε. For each rule count the a's and b's it adds: (1, 2), (0, 1) and (0, 0). We derive abbb and keep running totals n_a and n_b.
Use S → aSbb: it adds one a and two b's. Totals (1, 2).
Use S → bS: it adds one b. Totals (1, 3).
Use S → ε: S disappears and nothing is added. The string is abbb with totals (1, 3).
Let k be the number of times S → bS is used. Every aSbb adds (1, 2), so n_b = 2 n_a + k with k ≥ 0. Hence n_b ≥ 2 n_a for every string. Here 3 = 2 · 1 + 1.
Is n_b ≤ 2 n_a also true? No: S ⇒ bS ⇒ b has n_a = 0 and n_b = 1. Only n_b ≥ 2 n_a is an invariant of this grammar.
examples.answer: n_b ≥ 2 n_a. In general n_b = 2 n_a + k, where k is the number of uses of S → bS.

examples.setup: G: S → aaSb | aSbb | ε. Which statements hold for every string w in L(G)? (i) n_a + n_b is divisible by 3  (ii) n_a ≤ 2 n_b and n_b ≤ 2 n_a  (iii) n_a ≥ n_b
steps: Let x be the number of uses of aaSb, adding (2, 1), and y the uses of aSbb, adding (1, 2). Then n_a = 2x + y and n_b = x + 2y.
(i) n_a + n_b = 3(x + y), always divisible by 3. True.
(ii) n_a = 2x + y ≤ 2x + 4y = 2 n_b, and n_b = x + 2y ≤ 4x + 2y = 2 n_a. True.
(iii) With x = 0, y = 1 the string is abb with n_a = 1 and n_b = 2, so n_a < n_b. False.
examples.answer: (i) and (ii) are true, (iii) is false.

examples.setup: With the same grammar, the string baaabb has n_a = 3 and n_b = 3. Satisfying the count relations, is it in L(G)?
steps: Counts: 3 + 3 = 6 is divisible by 3, and 3 ≤ 6. It passes both necessary conditions.
Solve 2x + y = 3 and x + 2y = 3: x = y = 1, so the counts alone are consistent.
But both rules put their a's before their b's, so every derived string has the form a…ab…b. baaabb starts with b, so it is not derivable.
examples.answer: No. Count invariants are necessary, not sufficient: they cannot see the order of symbols.

cards.why: Count questions let you eliminate options quickly without naming the language. In GATE: pick the relation between the numbers of a's and b's that holds for all strings of a grammar, with a bound or a divisibility condition.
how: For each rule, write the pair (Δa, Δb).
Name the number of uses of each rule (x, y, k, …).
Write n_a and n_b in terms of them and combine into a relation.
Test the relation on the smallest strings, including ε and strings that use only one rule.
cards.mistake: Believing an invariant proves membership. Counts only exclude strings. Another slip is to claim the opposite inequality (n_b ≤ 2 n_a) when only one direction holds. Test a short string like b to catch that.
edge_cases: ε satisfies every invariant of the form 0 = 0 or 0 ≥ 0.
A rule that adds nothing to the counts (S → ε) never changes an invariant.
An invariant can be an equality (n_a = n_b), an inequality, or a divisibility fact.
connections: Naming the language (card 3) usually starts with the same per-rule additions.
Pumping-lemma proofs (next chapter) use the same idea of controlling counts.

objects.text: S → AB    A → aA | a    B → bB | b

steps.caption: Grammar G: S → AB, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. A derivation starts at the start symbol S and replaces one variable per step. Goal: derive aabb.
Step 1: S → AB. The form now has two variables, A and B.
Step 2: a leftmost derivation always replaces the leftmost variable. That is A, and we use A → aA.
Step 3: the leftmost variable is still A. Use A → a to finish it.
Step 4: now the only variable is B. Use B → bB.
Step 5: B → b. No variables are left, so aabb is derived in 5 steps and aabb is in L(G). This grammar generates a⁺b⁺: one or more a's, then one or more b's.

objects.text:
E → E+T | T    T → T*F | F    F → num
only the 14-tree is possible

steps.caption: Grammar: E → E+E | E*E | num. Take the input 2+3*4. A parse tree shows which rules were applied and how the string is grouped.
Parse tree 1: the root uses E → E*E. Its left E derives 2+3 and its right E derives 4.
Read the leaves left to right: 2+3*4. The tree says to add first, so its value is (2 + 3) * 4 = 20.
Parse tree 2 for the same string: the root uses E → E+E, and its right E derives 3*4.
Its value is 2 + (3 * 4) = 14. One string has two parse trees and two meanings, so the grammar is ambiguous.
Fix it by building precedence into the grammar: E → E+T | T, T → T*F | F, F → num. Now * can only sit lower in the tree than +, so only the 14-tree exists.

scenes.title: Reading the language of S → aSc | T, T → bTc | ε

objects.text: S → aSc | T      T → bTc | ε

steps.caption: To name the language of a grammar, say what each rule adds. G: S → aSc | T and T → bTc | ε. We derive abbccc and watch the counts.
S → aSc adds an a on the left and a c on the right, around the rest. This is an outer pair, so n = 1.
S → T stops adding outer pairs. From now on only T is rewritten, in the middle.
T → bTc adds a b on the left and a c on the right of the rest: an inner pair, so m = 1. The c's are now 2.
Use T → bTc again: m = 2. The string is now abbTccc, with 1 a, 2 b's and 3 c's.
T → ε removes the last variable: abbccc. Every a and every b has its own c, so the c's number n + m. L = { a^n b^m c^(n+m) : n, m ≥ 0 }.

scenes.title: Building a grammar for i = j or j = k

objects.text: L = { a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k }

steps.caption: Target: L = {a^i b^j c^k : i = j or j = k}. The word 'or' means union, so design each case on its own and join them at the end.
Case i = j: the matched core a^n b^n comes from A → aAb | ε, and the c's are free: C → cC | ε. Join them: S1 → A C.
Case j = k: the a's are free, B → aB | ε, and the matched core is b^n c^n, D → bDc | ε. Join them: S2 → B D.
Join the two cases with a union rule: S → S1 | S2.
Test aabbc (i = j = 2, k = 1): S ⇒ S1 ⇒ AC. A makes aabb and C makes c. In L.
Test abbcc (i = 1, j = k = 2): S ⇒ S2 ⇒ BD. B makes a and D makes bbcc. In L. A string like aabcc (i = 2, j = 1, k = 2) fits neither case and has no derivation.

scenes.title: A PDA accepting abcba, stack and input side by side

steps.caption: This PDA accepts { w c w^R }. State q0 pushes the first half, the symbol c switches to q1, and q1 matches the second half by popping. q2 is final. Input abcba, stack ⊥. A configuration is (state, unread input, stack with the top first).
Read a in q0: push A. The stack, top first, is A⊥.
Read b in q0: push B. The stack is BA⊥.
Read c: go to q1. The stack does not change, since c marks the middle.
Read b in q1 with B on top: they match, so pop B. The stack is A⊥.
Read a with A on top: they match, so pop A. The stack is ⊥ and the input is empty.
With the input used up and ⊥ on top, the ε-move goes to q2, a final state. Accepted, by final state.

objects.text: L = { w w^R }: no marker in the middle
stack after a, b:  ⊥ a b  (b on top)

steps.caption: L = {w w^R} is the even palindromes, with no marker in the middle. Take two members: abba and abbbba. Is there a deterministic way to read them?
A deterministic PDA pushes as it reads. After the first two symbols, a and b, the stack holds ⊥ a b with b on top, for both inputs.
The third symbol is b, equal to the top. In abba this b opens the second half, so the machine must pop.
In abbbba the very same b is still in the first half, since the middle comes after 3 symbols. Here the machine must push.
Up to this symbol the two inputs look identical (a, b, b), yet they need opposite moves. A deterministic machine must commit without seeing the future, so it fails on one of them.

An NPDA guesses the middle: it tries both moves and accepts if one branch works. So {w w^R} is context-free but not a DCFL. With a marker, {w c w^R}, the choice disappears and the PDA is deterministic.

set.text: NPDA only: CFL but not DCFL

steps.caption: L1 = {aⁿbⁿcᵐ}: a PDA matches the a's against the b's and ignores the c's. L1 is context-free.
L2 = {aᵐbⁿcⁿ}: the PDA ignores the a's and matches the b's against the c's. L2 is context-free too.
A string in both languages needs #a = #b (from L1) and #b = #c (from L2). That is the overlap: aⁿbⁿcⁿ.
aⁿbⁿcⁿ is not context-free, because one stack cannot compare three counts. Two CFLs gave a non-CFL, so CFLs are not closed under intersection.
Complement fails too. If CFLs were closed under complement, then L1 ∩ L2 = complement( complement(L1) ∪ complement(L2) ) would be context-free, since union is closed. It is not.
A safe case: a CFL intersected with a regular language is context-free. Run the PDA and a DFA together; the stack is still the only unbounded memory.

scenes.title: Converting S → aSb | ab to CNF and counting steps

steps.caption: Original grammar G: S → aSb | ab. Chomsky normal form (CNF) allows only rules A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal).
Step 1: give each terminal its own variable, A → a and B → b. The rules become S → ASB | AB, A → a, B → b.

set.text:
S → ASB | AB
A → a    B → b

steps.caption: Step 2: break the long rule ASB into pieces of two variables with X → SB, so S → AX. CNF: S → AX | AB, X → SB, A → a, B → b.

set.text:
S → AX | AB    X → SB
A → a    B → b

steps.caption: Derive aabb in the CNF grammar. Steps 1 to 3: S ⇒ AX ⇒ aX ⇒ aSB. The form is a S B after 3 steps.
Steps 4 and 5: aSB ⇒ aABB ⇒ aaBB, using S → AB and then A → a.
Steps 6 and 7: aaBB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb. Total 7 = 2n − 1 for n = 4: three binary steps (n − 1) and four terminal steps (n).
Greibach normal form (GNF) needs every rule to start with a terminal: S → aSB | aB, B → b. Each step now produces one terminal, so aabb takes 4 steps: S ⇒ aSB ⇒ aaBB ⇒ aabB ⇒ aabb.

Length 1: a cell holds the variables with a rule X → terminal. Each a gives {A} and each b gives {B}.
Length 2: split into 1 + 1 and look for a rule X → YZ. aa: A A has no rule, so ∅. ab: A B gives S, so {S}. bb: B B has no rule, so ∅.
Length 3: aab splits as a|ab = A,S and aa|b = ∅,B. No rule X → A S, so ∅. abb splits as a|bb = A,∅ and ab|b = S,B, and C → SB gives {C}.
Length 4: aabb splits as a|abb = A,C and S → AC gives S. The other splits, aa|bb and aab|b, contain ∅. So the cell is {S}.
The top cell contains S, so aabb is in the language. Cost for n = 4: n(n+1)/2 = 10 cells and 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 split checks. In general this is O(n³).

scenes.title: Tracking n_a and n_b for S → aSbb | bS | ε

steps.caption: Grammar S → aSbb | bS | ε. For each rule count the a's and b's it adds: (1, 2), (0, 1) and (0, 0). We derive abbb and keep running totals n_a and n_b.
Use S → aSbb: it adds one a and two b's. Totals (1, 2).
Use S → bS: it adds one b. Totals (1, 3).
Use S → ε: S disappears and nothing is added. The string is abbb with totals (1, 3).
Let k be the number of times S → bS is used. Every aSbb adds (1, 2), so n_b = 2 n_a + k with k ≥ 0. Hence n_b ≥ 2 n_a for every string. Here 3 = 2 · 1 + 1.
Is n_b ≤ 2 n_a also true? No: S ⇒ bS ⇒ b has n_a = 0 and n_b = 1. Only n_b ≥ 2 n_a is an invariant of this grammar.
